claim: Independent random errors average out: Galton's 787 ox-weight cards gave a median 1207 lb vs truth 1198 and a mean of 1197 (Wallis 2014). One data set, but the founding case.
agent_test: Replay on numeric estimation: mean of N independent samples vs single sample, equal tokens.

claim: A majority vote beats a single voter when each voter is right more than half the time and errors are independent (Condorcet: n=3, p=0.8 gives 0.896); with p below 0.5 more voters make it worse. Correlated errors shrink the gain below the independent limit (a 9-judge LLM panel acts like about 2 independent votes, Kohli 2026).
agent_test: Measure per-item pairwise error agreement of our samples; compare vote gain to the independent-binomial prediction.
audit_note: 0.896 is correct, and the arXiv papers support correlation capping the gain (Kohli: 9 judges give about 2 independent votes), but Condorcet's theorem states independence plus p>0.5 as a sufficient condition for majority gain, not 'only if'; the claim's own second sentence concedes correlated voters can still gain.
claim_before_audit: A majority vote beats a single voter only if each voter is right more than half the time and errors are independent (Condorcet: n=3, p=0.8 gives 0.896). Correlation caps the gain below the independent limit.

claim: LLM errors are strongly correlated across models: about 60% agreement when both err (HELM), pair agreement up to 0.97 for sibling models; correlation rises with shared provider, architecture and accuracy.
agent_test: Compute error agreement between our scaffold samples and between model variants before trusting any vote.
audit_note: Kim et al. report ~60% agreement when both err on HELM, 0.97 for two Llama siblings, and higher correlation for same provider/architecture and for more accurate models; Goel et al. independently support error overlap rising with capability.

claim: Effective number of independent LLM voters is far below the nominal count: 9 judges give Kish n_eff about 2.2; 20k-item VLM ensembles give a participation ratio of 2.86.
agent_test: Report n_eff for each vote; cap claimed gain at n_eff.

claim: Sampling-and-voting helps a lot where a checkable answer string exists: self-consistency +17.9 GSM8K; Agent Forest +12 to +24 GSM8K at 40 agents, gains shrink near ceiling and on hard items.
agent_test: Majority over k samples vs greedy at equal tokens on math/code items with exact answers.
audit_note: Gain near ceiling is only implicit in sources; hard-item taper appears in Agent Forest's synthetic difficulty scan.

claim: Plurality voting fails when verification is absent: shared misconceptions get reinforced; at 25x cost no consistent gain on truthfulness benchmarks; the top wrong answer is 65-87% of wrong MATH responses.
agent_test: On items with no verifier, compare vote to single sample; expect no gain, route to verification instead.
audit_note: The 25x/no-consistent-gain and 65-87% figures come only from Denisov-Blanch et al. (a18 and a19 are the same paper); other listed sources (Kohli, Shu) only corroborate correlated errors generally and are not truthfulness-benchmark evidence.

claim: Heterogeneous crowds beat clones: homogeneous model groups showed no deliberation gain (d 0.06-0.14) vs heterogeneous d=0.26-0.40; LLM crowds flatten with group size while human groups keep gaining; different-family models lower correlation (0.53 vs 0.67).
agent_test: Diversify via different prompts/frames/personas and measure correlation drop vs same-prompt resampling.
audit_note: Effect-size ranges mix studies (homogeneous d 0.06-0.14 is Study 1; later study homogeneous d 0.01-0.10, heterogeneous 0.26 vs 0.40 in Study 1); meaning unchanged.

claim: Diversity is not free: mixing different LLMs (Mixed-MoA) lost to single-best-model Self-MoA by 6.6 points AlpacaEval and 3.8% average; quality matters more than variety when quality gaps are large. Diversity only helps if members are individually good.
agent_test: Compare diverse-weak vs repeated-best-sample ensembles at equal tokens.
claim_note: Gap search: mixing wins only at matched quality (d04 +0.027 at k=3, d12 regression quality coefficient larger than diversity coefficient on all three tasks) and only with a good selector (d07). Still contested on transfer to one model in different roles.

claim: Hong-Page diversity-beats-ability holds only under strong assumptions (finite heuristic pool, identical perspectives); the theorem concerns search, not voting on a fact.
agent_test: Test on search tasks: random-strategy team vs best-strategy team at equal tokens.

claim: Social influence can erode crowd accuracy: in Lorenz 2011 the wisdom indicator fell about one unit and confidence rose without accuracy gain; but in decentralised networks (Becker 2017) mean error fell 10% and in Almaatouq 2021 influence helps under some weights. Direction depends on network and who is central.
agent_test: In multi-sample revision, hide peer answers in round 1 and compare to shared-answer revision.
claim_note: Gap search: Bertalanic 2026 adds a harm case for LLM agents shown peer answers (Ministral GSM-Hard 20.7 vs 48.3 blind). Direction for LLMs leans to harm; human network results stay mixed.

claim: In tested settings, multi-agent debate does not reliably beat simple majority voting: on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, mean accuracy over 7 benchmarks was 0.7691 for majority voting vs 0.7377 for decentralized debate at T=2 (Debate or Vote, 2508.17536), whose martingale analysis says debate alone leaves expected correctness unchanged; Smit et al. (2024) find debate systems do not reliably outperform self-consistency (though tuned variants may), and Wynn et al. (2025) report debate can lower accuracy by flipping correct answers to incorrect.
agent_test: Equal-token comparison of k-sample vote vs k-agent debate.
audit_note: Voting beating debate (0.7691 vs 0.7377) is a Qwen2.5-7B result averaged over 7 benchmarks; Smit et al. say debate only 'does not reliably outperform' voting/self-consistency and that tuned MAD (e.g. Multi-Persona) can do better, so a general 'not better than voting' is too strong.
claim_before_audit: Debate between agents is not better than voting: martingale analysis and benchmarks show voting beats debate (0.769 vs 0.738 at T=2 on Qwen2.5-7B); debate rounds can flip correct answers to wrong.

claim: Within-person averaging (crowd within) works: two guesses averaged beat the first by dz 0.40 immediate and up to 0.34 delayed; second guesses are worse than first. Earlier immediate replications were mixed (2 clear, 1 borderline, 1 fail).
agent_test: Compare average of two spaced/reframed samples vs one; delay equals changed context in agent.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Aggregator choice matters when errors are skewed: arithmetic mean was +323% off on Swiss murders while median/geometric mean were within 15%; Galton's mean beat median once, so no universal rule.
agent_test: Use median/geometric mean for numeric answers with order-of-magnitude outliers.
claim_note: Gap search: median of 30 samples beat mean, mode and greedy on LLM numeric guesstimation (d06), consistent with skew-robust aggregators.
audit_note: The 323%/within-15% comparison is for the murders item only; on other Lorenz items median and geometric mean were far off too (e.g. rapes -55%/-61%), which supports 'no universal rule'.

claim: Smarter aggregation can beat plain majority but needs data: Surprisingly Popular cut error 21-24%; learned logistic aggregator Brier 0.241 vs mean 0.313 (Douven); OW/ML methods need training samples or many models.
agent_test: Only usable if we have labelled history; otherwise default to median plus verification.
audit_note: SP percentages (21.3/24.2/22.2) were verified only through secondary coverage (Wikipedia, MIT press), not the Nature full text; Douven's 0.241 vs 0.313 is on the 94-item clean subset with aggregators trained on the other 160 items; SP is a human-crowd result.

claim: LLM crowd of 12 different models matched a 925-human forecasting crowd (Brier 0.20 vs 0.19, n=31 questions), but with acquiescence bias; equivalence test exploratory.
agent_test: Debias mean toward 50% or extremize; check calibration on our forecast items.

claim: Data contamination inflates LLM crowd skill: cloud-vs-local gap drops from 35.8% to 8.9% on a clean subset, and models stay below the market at their cutoff.
agent_test: Use post-cutoff or generated items when benchmarking crowd gains.

claim: Showing a model an external crowd median improved Brier 17-28%, but less than averaging; models anchor in proportion to distance.
agent_test: Test anchoring: give the agent a prior estimate and measure copy rate.

claim: Clustering models by reasoning behaviour can cut calls 88% with accuracy about as good as full crowd; but selected line-up was only at the 83-88th percentile of random line-ups, and farthest-apart voting was worse than random.
agent_test: Not directly applicable; use behaviour-based, not label-based, diversity measures.

claim: Vote vs consensus depends on task: voting +13.2% on reasoning, consensus +2.8% on knowledge tasks.
agent_test: Test vote vs consensus by task type.

claim: Prompt, persona or rephrasing diversity on one model does not reliably beat plain temperature sampling for plain voting. Where error correlation is already near zero (AIMO 3, mean -0.258), diverse prompts cost 0.3 to 3.7 points. Persona frames cut error correlation (0.388 vs 0.461) but no equal-token comparison against same-prompt sampling exists.
agent_test: Measure pairwise error correlation of k temperature samples first; only add frames if rho above about 0.1 and per-frame accuracy stays within a few points.

claim: For a vote with correlated members the ceiling is set by the shared-error rate, not by k. Beta-binomial calculation at per-vote accuracy 0.69: rho=0.1 gives ceiling 0.887, rho=0.2 gives 0.805, versus 1.0 at independence. Across 67 models the all-wrong rate was 0.052 on MATH-500 and pairwise rho does not identify it.
agent_test: Estimate rho and all-wrong rate on our item set; cap k where the curve flattens (about 20 at rho 0.1).
audit_note: I reproduced the beta-binomial ceilings independently (0.887 at rho=0.1, 0.805 at rho=0.2 for p=0.69); beta=0.052 on MATH-500 rests on only 17 all-wrong events (CP 0.030-0.081); Kaniovski and Zaigraev was read only via search snippets, and the exchangeable beta-binomial model is an assumption.

claim: Spending extra tokens on a strong, accurate selector or verifier can beat more same-source votes: in Shu (2026, MATH-500, n=570, k=7) a strong different-model verifier gained +24.2 pp on pivotal items versus 0.0 pp for an extra same-source draw, but a role-reversed verifier lost 11.2 pp, so verifier strength rather than a different build is the active ingredient; in Maryanskyy et al. judge selection reached a 0.810 win rate vs 0.496 for voting and 0.179 for synthesis, which fell to about 0.50-0.61 with decoupled judges.
agent_test: On an unverifiable item, run k votes, and only when the split is 3-4 of 7 call a separate verifier or judge; test against 2k extra votes at equal tokens.
audit_note: Numbers match (+24.2 pp, 0.0 pp same-source, -11.2 pp; win rates 0.810/0.496/0.179), but Shu's own post-mortem says the different-model vs same-source contrast confounds provenance with verifier strength (role-reversed different-model verifier hurt), and Maryanskyy's judge-selection 0.810 falls to 0.611 or 0.500 when judges are decoupled from the generators, so 'a verifier from a different build' is not what the sources show.
claim_before_audit: Without a verifier, extra tokens are better spent on a selector or verifier from a different build than on more same-model votes. Same-source extra vote gained 0.0 pp while a strong verifier gained +24.2 pp on pivotal items; judge selection won 0.810 vs vote 0.496 and synthesis 0.179. A weak verifier hurts (-11.2 pp).

claim: Whether synthesis beats voting is unsettled. One model with rephrased questions: trace-level synthesis beat voting at similar call count (AIME 91.1 vs 85.6, GPQA 73.2 vs 70.7). Across different models, synthesis lost badly to judge selection (0.179 vs 0.810).
agent_test: Test synthesis vs judge selection vs vote on the same item set, equal tokens.

claim: Showing earlier answers to a later revision hurts compared with blind revision: isolated self-correction beat peer-visible debate by up to 27.6 pp (Ministral GSM-Hard 48.3 vs 20.7), random unrelated rationales did as well as peers, and agents adopted the majority answer 85.5% of the time (Qwen MMLU-Hard).
agent_test: Keep revision blind to prior sample answers; test showing only the critique, not the answer.

claim: Own-confidence signals are weak truth signals but useful for saving samples. Within-question discrimination was 52.2% to 62.3% (chance 50%); confidence-weighted voting with the best signal (P(True)) cut samples by 41% to 46% (other confidence signals 10% to 31%); adaptive stopping cut the sample budget by 3.3x on average and up to 7.9x with an average accuracy drop below 0.1%. All on checkable-answer tasks, and agreement cannot detect a shared error.
agent_test: Use agreement fraction for stopping on easy items; do not use confidence to resolve a shared-error split.
audit_note: Within-question discrimination 52.2% to 62.3% and the 7.9x / under 0.1% adaptive-stopping figures match, but the ~40% sample saving is only for the best confidence method P(True) (41% at budget 5, 46% at 10); other methods cut 10-31%, and 7.9x is the best case on one dataset (3.3x on average).
claim_before_audit: Own-confidence signals are weak truth signals but useful for saving samples. Within-question discrimination was 52.2% to 62.3% (chance 50%); confidence-weighted voting cut samples 40% on average; adaptive stopping cut budget up to 7.9x with under 0.1% accuracy loss. All on checkable-answer tasks, and agreement cannot detect a shared error.

claim: For numeric estimates from one LLM, the median of sampled reasoning paths beats mean, mode and greedy; median of 5 beat self-consistency with 30 on two question sets. Reframed-versus-same-prompt averaging (crowd-within delay) remains untested.
agent_test: Use median of 5 samples for numeric answers; test reframed samples against same-prompt samples.
